question: A 25-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 30 minutes after he was involved in a motorcycle collision. He was not wearing a helmet. Physical examination shows left periorbital ecchymosis. A CT scan of the head shows a fracture of the greater wing of the left sphenoid bone with compression of the left superior orbital fissure. Physical examination of this patient is most likely to show which of the following findings?

enhanced_information: In the case of a fracture of the greater wing of the left sphenoid bone with compression of the left superior orbital fissure, the cranial nerves most likely affected are III, IV, V1, and VI. This can lead to ophthalmoplegia, which includes impaired eye movements and potentially an absent corneal reflex due to V1 involvement. Numbness of the left cheek is unlikely as it involves the V2 branch, not V1. Preserved left lateral gaze is unlikely due to potential impairment of cranial nerve VI, which controls lateral rectus muscle movement. Complete loss of vision is unlikely as the optic nerve (CN II) is not typically involved in superior orbital fissure syndrome. Decreased sense of smell is also unlikely as the olfactory nerve (CN I) is not involved. Therefore, the most likely finding is an absent left corneal reflex due to V1 involvement.
analysis: In this scenario, the patient has a fracture of the greater wing of the left sphenoid bone with compression of the left superior orbital fissure. The superior orbital fissure is a key anatomical structure through which cranial nerves III (oculomotor), IV (trochlear), V1 (ophthalmic branch of the trigeminal nerve), and VI (abducens) pass. Compression in this area can lead to superior orbital fissure syndrome, which typically presents with ophthalmoplegia (paralysis or weakness of the eye muscles), ptosis (drooping of the eyelid), and sensory loss in the distribution of the V1 nerve, which includes the forehead and corneal reflex. The absent left corneal reflex is due to the involvement of the ophthalmic branch of the trigeminal nerve (V1), which is responsible for the sensory component of the corneal reflex. Other options such as decreased sense of smell, numbness of the left cheek, preserved left lateral gaze, and complete loss of vision of the left eye are less likely based on the nerves affected by the superior orbital fissure compression. Therefore, the most likely finding in this patient is an absent left corneal reflex.
